title: Committee of Privileges Report (Recommendations in respect of Ms Raeesah Khan) and Committee of Privileges Report (Recommendations in respect of Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Faisal Manap and Ms Sylvia Lim)
what_it_is: Committee of Privileges Report (Recommendations in respect of Ms Raeesah Khan) and Committee of Privileges Report (Recommendations in respect of Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Faisal Manap and Ms Sylvia Lim)

sections.label: Motions moved together
sections.summary: The Speaker allows both Motions to be moved and debated together, and moves the Second Motion on the Committee of Privileges Report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: In view of the earlier decision of this House to have both Motions taken together and the debate to proceed simultaneously on both Motions, I will allow the Motions to be so moved.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I also beg to move the Second Motion standing in my name on today's Order Paper titled "Committee of Privileges Report (Recommendations in respect of Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Faisal Manap and Ms Sylvia Lim)".

sections.label: Khan's untruth and Committee report
sections.summary: Ms Khan confessed in Parliament to the Untruth, a complaint was referred to the Committee of Privileges, which reported on 10 February 2022.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Ms Khan made that statement twice on 3 August and repeated it during a later session on 4 October.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: However, on 1 November 2021, Ms Khan confessed in Parliament that she had not, in fact, accompanied the survivor to the Police station.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I will refer to this as "the Untruth".

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I raised a complaint under Standing Order 100(7)(b) against Ms Khan for breaches of privilege and the matter was referred to the Committee of Privileges (the Committee).

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee completed its work and presented its Report to Parliament on 10 February 2022, making findings and recommendations in respect of Ms Raeesah Khan’s conduct.

sections.label: Fine recommended for Khan
sections.summary: The Committee recommended a $25,000 fine, half the maximum penalty, on Ms Khan for lying twice on 3 August.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee has accordingly recommended that a fine of $25,000 – that is, half of the maximum penalty – be imposed on Ms Khan for lying twice on 3 August.

sections.label: Committee findings on leaders
sections.summary: The Committee found Ms Khan truthful and that Mr Pritam Singh, and to a lesser extent Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap, lied to it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Taking all these into account, the Committee found that Ms Raeesah Khan was telling the truth and that Mr Pritam Singh, and to a lesser extent, Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Faisal Manap, had lied to the Committee.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: (a) Immediately after the 8 August meeting, Ms Khan sent a WhatsApp message to her assistants, stating “they’ve", meaning Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap, "agreed that the best thing to do is to take the information to the grave”.

sections.label: Finding on 3 October meeting
sections.summary: The Committee found clear evidence that Mr Singh strongly pointed Ms Khan towards continuing the Untruth on 3 October.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: As to the 3 October meeting, the Committee found “the evidence was quite clear that Mr Singh strongly pointed Ms Khan towards continuing with the Untruth on 3 October”.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: (a) On 3 October, Mr Singh visited Ms Khan at her home specifically to advise her on what to say at the 4 October Parliamentary Sitting because he “had a feeling” that the topic might come up.

sections.label: Mitigation and lower fine
sections.summary: The Committee found Ms Khan's culpability mitigated and recommended a lower $10,000 fine for repeating the Untruth on 4 October 2021.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee therefore found that Ms Khan’s culpability in respect of her repetition of the Untruth on 4 October was mitigated by the following: (a) the fact that she was a first-time MP who confessed to and sought guidance from her Party leaders as to what to do; (b) regrettably, the guidance they gave, and which she followed, was to maintain the lie; and (c) her conduct and evidence showed that she would have come clean, if she had been advised to do so from 8 August.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee also took into account that Ms Khan's mental health had been "unfairly and publicly attacked, in particular, by Mr Singh", and that Ms Khan had resigned as a Member of Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee has, therefore, recommended a lower fine of $10,000 in respect of the repetition of the Untruth on 4 October 2021.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This is dealt with in paragraph 2(c) of the First Motion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Based on the objective evidence before the Committee, the Committee made these findings: (a) that all three senior Workers' Party leaders have lied to the Committee as to what was discussed at the 8 August meeting, and that they guided Ms Khan to maintain the Untruth she had told; (b) that Mr Singh lied about what had happened at the 3 October meeting and essentially gave Ms Khan to understand that it would be all right to maintain the Untruth if the matter came up in Parliament the next day.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In addition, Mr Faisal Manap refused to answer a question from the Committee at least eight times, despite being reminded that he had been called before the Committee to assist with its investigations, and that his refusal would amount to an offence and constitute a contempt of Parliament.

sections.label: Referral of Singh to Public Prosecutor
sections.summary: The Committee recommended that Parliament refer Mr Singh's conduct to the Public Prosecutor to consider criminal proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee has therefore recommended that Parliament refer Mr Singh's conduct to the Public Prosecutor (PP), with a view to considering whether to institute criminal proceedings.

sections.label: Faisal Manap referral and deferred PPIPA offences
sections.summary: The Committee recommended referring Mr Faisal Manap to the PP and deferring action on other PPIPA offences pending criminal proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In the case of Mr Faisal Manap, his refusal to produce documents or answer questions can also amount to an offence under the PPIPA, and that is the Part 5 offence, so the Committee has recommended that he also be referred to the PP.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Apart from the offences to be referred to the PP, there remain the following potential offences under the PPIPA that need to be dealt with by Parliament: (a)	Dishonourable conduct and contempt of Parliament on the part of Mr Pritam Singh, for lying to the Committee, and for his role in guiding Ms Khan to lie to Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee has recommended that Parliament defer any action on this until the criminal proceedings (if any) are completed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: (b)	Dishonourable conduct and contempt of Parliament on the part of Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Faisal Manap for lying about the 8 August meeting and for their initial concurrence in the guidance to maintain the lie by agreeing that it should be taken to the grave.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Likewise, the Committee has recommended that any decision on this be deferred until the outcome of the referral of Mr Singh's conduct to the PP.

sections.label: Two Motions on Committee of Privileges Report
sections.summary: Two Questions were moved by the Leader of the House on the Committee of Privileges Report recommendations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The first Question is as moved by Leader of the House on the Motion titled "Committee of Privileges Report (Recommendations in respect of Ms Raeesah Khan)".

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The second Question is as moved by Leader of the House on the Motion titled "Committee of Privileges Report (Recommendations in respect of Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Faisal Manap and Ms Sylvia Lim)".

sections.label: Separate votes and disallowed amendments
sections.summary: The Speaker will put questions on both Motions separately and disallow amendments that negative or nullify the other Motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: At the end of the debate, I will put the questions on both Motions separately so that the House can express its vote on each Motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: In addition, I will also disallow any amendment to either Motion that has the effect of negativing or nullifying the other Motion.

sections.label: Denial of instructing Khan to lie
sections.summary: The speaker states he never instructed Ms Khan to hide the truth and no leaders told her to take her lie to the grave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: At no time did I instruct Ms Khan to hide the truth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: At the meeting on August 8, none of the three Workers' Party leaders told Ms Khan to take her lie to the grave.

sections.label: Objection to weaponising psychiatric evaluation conclusion
sections.summary: The speaker calls the conclusion that he weaponised Ms Khan's condition in seeking a psychiatric evaluation the most egregious.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The most egregious, in my mind, is the conclusion that in seeking a psychiatric evaluation from Ms Khan, I had somehow weaponised her condition.

sections.label: Mitigation for Ms Khan's condition
sections.summary: The speaker says Ms Khan should not be excessively punished for a condition and that the COP ignored this mitigatory evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I believe that Ms Khan should not be excessively punished for a condition she could be labouring under and the COP ought to see it as a mitigatory point in her favour.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This evidence of mine, supported by the COP's Minutes of Evidence on culpability and proportionality, is ignored by the COP.

sections.label: Khan resignation and Loh's view
sections.summary: Ms Khan said she would respect the Disciplinary Panel's decision, while Ms Loh said resignation should not be on the cards.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Ms Khan, in her own WhatsApp text to me on 22 November at Annex C-29, states that she would respect any decision the Disciplinary Panel (DP) makes, even if it is to resign.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In my DP notes of 25 November covering the meeting with Ms Loh and Mr Nathan which, again, was submitted to the COP, Ms Loh made it clear that Ms Khan's resignation should not be on the cards because, in her view, what she did in Parliament was not serious and it was not as if Ms Khan had "laundered money".

sections.label: Loh and Nathan WhatsApp replies
sections.summary: Ms Loh and Mr Nathan's contemporaneous WhatsApp replies are cited as contradicting the COP's findings at paragraph 93.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For the record, Ms Loh's contemporaneous reply upon receiving my message was: "I see.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Is there something you need me to do?" Mr Nathan's reply was clearer: "Hi, Pritam: Noted on this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I know it's difficult, but I think party members and supporters will be comforted by it." These contemporaneous WhatsApp messages directly contradict the COP's findings at paragraph 93.

sections.label: Candidate selection and COP findings
sections.summary: The speaker will finetune Workers' Party candidate selection, takes responsibility for wrong decisions, and rejects the COP's findings against him and other MPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the main, our candidate selection processes can always be better in spite of the extraordinary circumstances and the political culture of a one-party dominant state.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I will confer with my colleagues with a view to finetune the processes in the Workers' Party as best as we can, taking into account the structural challenges we in the Opposition face.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Of course, I will endeavour to the best of my abilities to ensure that our candidates are rational, responsible and respectable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And if any candidate selection decisions are wrong, I, as Secretary General of the party, take full responsibility.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: On the Second Motion, I am unable to accept the COP's findings that offences have been committed under the Parliament Act by me or any other Workers' Party MPs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Nevertheless, should Parliament resolve to adopt the Motion, I intend to clear my name and will cooperate fully with the Public Prosecutor.

sections.label: Khan confesses untruth in Parliament
sections.summary: On 8 August, Ms Khan went to Mr Singh, Mr Faisal Manap and Ms Lim and confessed to speaking an untruth in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: On 8 August, Ms Khan went to Mr Singh, Mr Faisal Manap and Ms Lim, confessed to speaking an untruth in Parliament.

sections.label: No discussion after 8 August meeting
sections.summary: By their own admission, in the almost two months after the 8 August meeting, there was no discussion and no one spoke to each other.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: By their own admission, in the almost two months that followed the meeting on 8 August, there was no discussion, no one spoke to each other.

sections.label: Khan texted Singh on 4 October
sections.summary: The passage asks why Ms Khan texted Mr Singh asking what she should do on 4 October, and says she continued with the narrative and the lie.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: If he had been so clear with Ms Khan, why is it then on 4 October, when Minister Shanmugam raised the matter, Ms Khan texted Mr Singh, "What should I do, Pritam?" So, she continued with what she was told to do: continue with the narrative, continue with the lie.

sections.label: Clarifying the second lie in Parliament
sections.summary: The passage asks why it was not made clear that Ms Khan needed to return to Parliament and clarify the second lie immediately.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Again, why not, at that point, make it clear that she needed to come back to Parliament now and clarify?

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: And why not at that point, ensure that the second lie in Parliament, the one which he, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap were aware of to be a lie, be clarified immediately?

sections.label: Loh and Nathan spoke to Singh
sections.summary: The Committee of Privileges heard from Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudhishthra Nathan, who both spoke to Mr Singh independently on 12 October about his 3 October discussion with Ms Khan.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: On top of this, the Committee of Privileges heard from Ms Loh Pei Ying and Mr Yudhishthra Nathan.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: They both spoke to Mr Singh independently on 12 October, when he gave an account of what he had discussed with Ms Khan on 3 October.

sections.label: Singh's words to Khan
sections.summary: Mr Singh himself described what he had said to Ms Khan on 3 October as, "It was your call".

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Mr Singh himself had described what he had said to Ms Khan on 3 October as, "It was your call".

sections.label: Singh's assurance and 12 October evidence
sections.summary: The passage says Mr Singh's assurance meant follow the guidance and continue with the lie, and that 12 October was the first time Ms Khan was told to tell the truth in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: It underscores the idea that Mr Singh meant on 3 October when he assured her he would not judge her: follow the guidance, continue with the lie, there will be no judgement.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: It was Mr Singh's own evidence that 12 October was the first time that Ms Khan was told that she should come to Parliament and tell the truth.

sections.label: Singh changed evidence several times
sections.summary: The passage states that Mr Singh changed his evidence before the Committee of Privileges on this key point several times.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Members will also remember that Mr Singh changed his evidence before the Committee of Privileges on this key point several times.

sections.label: Committee finds Singh lied
sections.summary: The Committee of Privileges concluded that Singh lied, a serious transgression ordinarily requiring investigation leading to exoneration or prosecution.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Most reasonable people admit a serious possibility that he might have lied.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: And the Committee of Privileges has come to the conclusion that he did, indeed, lie, a serious transgression that, ordinarily, would require an investigation, leading either to exoneration or prosecution.

sections.label: No normalising political lying
sections.summary: Lying by politicians cannot be normalised or rewarded, and only a clear resolution will restore trust in the political process.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: First, we cannot normalise lying by politicians or, even worse, reward it.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Only a clear and unambiguous resolution will restore trust in the political process.

sections.label: Alleged Singh deception unresolved
sections.summary: The allegation that Singh deceived his party, the public and Parliament under oath must be dealt with unambiguously, if necessary by the Courts.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: Third, Mr Speaker, the allegation that Mr Singh planned and executed, what sounds like a ruthless deception of his party, the public and Parliament, under oath to the Select Committee and then, possibly, threw his own party cadres under the bus when they exposed him, it cannot be left to fester unresolved, weakening trust in politics, politicians and this institution.

sentences.speaker: The Government Whip (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
sentences.text: It must be dealt with unambiguously and, if necessary, by the Courts with neither fear nor favour, for the sake of our democratic institutions.

sections.label: Singh's weaponised condition remark
sections.summary: As a Committee member, the speaker heard Singh say he had somehow weaponised her condition, referring to findings on Ms Khan's mental health.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: As a Member of the Committee of Privileges, I heard Mr Singh say earlier, very specifically, that, I quote, "I had somehow weaponised her condition", referring, I presume, to the Committee of Privileges' findings on what he had said about Ms Khan's purported mental health conditions; "weaponised her condition".

sections.label: Weaponised term not in Report
sections.summary: The term weaponised does not appear in the Report, so the speaker asks the Leader of the Opposition who told him it was used.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: If, indeed, that word was not used and it was not right for me to use it, I am happy to withdraw it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But let me just, at least, look at the Report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: And, so, it does not appear anywhere in the Report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: So, I would like to ask the Leader of the Opposition, who told him about the use of the term "weaponised" with respect to Ms Khan's mental health condition?

sections.label: Parliament at democracy's apex
sections.summary: Parliament sits at the apex of democracy, discussing state matters, enacting laws, voting money, with Government answering and Opposition holding it to account.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Parliament sits at the apex of our system of democracy.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: It is where the most important matters of state are discussed, laws are enacted, supplies of money are voted, with the Government setting the direction and proposing policies, while answering to the public through Parliament and the Opposition holding the Government to account while also being a government-in-waiting should the ruling party lose the support of the people.

sections.label: Truth and right action
sections.summary: Calls for always telling the truth and doing the right thing by Singapore, especially when hard or awkward.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Tell the truth always and do the right thing by Singapore, even when it is hard or awkward; in fact, especially when it is hard or awkward.

sections.label: MPs' integrity and loyalty
sections.summary: States MPs must have integrity, put duty before self and country before party, with ultimate loyalty to Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: MPs must be people with integrity at their core, who speak and act in an upright manner, always putting duty before self, and country before party.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And our highest duty – our ultimate loyalty – is not to our party, but to Singapore.

sections.label: Israel's government formation difficulty
sections.summary: Says Ben-Gurion's Israel has become one that can barely form a government despite four elections in two years.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Ben-Gurion's Israel has morphed into one which can barely form a government, despite four general elections in two years.

sections.label: Lee Kuan Yew rejecting one-party state
sections.summary: Recalls Lee Kuan Yew explaining he could have made a one-party state but chose not to, fearing complacency.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew once explained at that time, with the PAP completely dominant, he could have changed the Constitution and made this a one-party state.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But he deliberately chose not to because he knew that, without the need to contest and win elections, the governing party would, over time, become complacent and flabby and that would be disastrous for Singapore.

sections.label: Lancet study on trust and corruption
sections.summary: Cites a Lancet study finding high trust and low corruption linked to lower infection rates and higher vaccine coverage.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I have been saying this for two years but, recently, there was a study published in the Lancet, a British medical journal, which confirmed this.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: It studied multiple countries and found that countries with high levels of trust and, together with low corruption, saw lower infection rates and higher vaccine coverage because the people's trust in government and their trust in one another made much more difference to the outcome than the resources spent on healthcare and even whether they had a universal healthcare system or not.

sections.label: UK government trust breakdown
sections.summary: Says the UK government, by ignoring its own rules, caused a severe breakdown of trust and lost credibility in COVID-19 controls.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: By ignoring its own rules, the current UK government has caused a severe breakdown of trust and lost credibility in its COVID-19 controls.

sections.label: Raeesah Khan lying in Parliament
sections.summary: Ms Raeesah Khan lied in Parliament twice on 3 August last year and again on 4 October.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Ms Raeesah Khan lied in Parliament twice on 3 August last year and the third time when questioned two months later on 4 October.

sections.label: Workers' Party leaders' instruction question
sections.summary: The question is whether three Workers' Party leaders instructed Ms Khan to continue her lie in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: First, whether the three Workers' Party leaders, Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Faisal Manap and Ms Sylvia Lim, had instructed Ms Khan to continue with her lie in Parliament.

sections.label: Committee assessment of deliberate untruths
sections.summary: The Committee assessed the untruths as deliberate premeditated acts to mislead, amounting to perjury if proven in Court.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The Committee's assessment is that these untruths were not accidental or incidental errors but deliberate premeditated acts done with a definite intent to mislead and to deceive.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: They are not just breaches of parliamentary privilege but, if proven in Court, they amount to perjury, lying under oath, and perjury is a serious criminal offence.

sections.label: Referring matter to Public Prosecutor
sections.summary: The speaker believes the Committee's recommendation is best and urges referring the matter to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In fact, they are already insinuating this as a smokescreen to obscure the real issue, that the Workers' Party had lied while under solemn oath.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I believe, therefore, that what the Committee recommends is the best way forward.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Since a criminal offence appears to have been committed, let Parliament refer the matter to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Let the Public Prosecutor consider the evidence afresh.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: If the charges are filed, Mr Pritam Singh and also Mr Faisal Manap can defend themselves in Court.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The Court will have to be satisfied that their guilt has been established beyond reasonable doubt and, if they are innocent, they have nothing to fear.

sections.label: Party leader on upholding standards
sections.summary: The speaker says his duty is to maximise chances that whichever party wins upholds the same high standards of conduct and honesty.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: My job as party leader is to make sure the PAP governs well to the best of its ability, so that it retains the mandate of the people for as many elections as possible.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But my duty as the leader of the country is also to maximise the chances that whichever party wins future elections, it will uphold and be held to the same high standards of proper conduct and honesty as the PAP, so that our democratic system can continue to operate properly, whichever party is in charge, and would not go down the drain.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: With our lives and future at stake, everyone participating in the system must be held to the same standards.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: There can be no excuses, no double standards and no pardoning of inexcusable behaviour, just because the offending party portrays itself as the underdog.

sections.label: Absence of admission of wrongdoing
sections.summary: The speaker finds most disappointing the complete absence of any admission that the three MPs have done anything wrong.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: What I personally find most disappointing in the Workers' Party narrative and in their response, including in this House today, is the complete absence of any admission that the three MPs have done anything wrong.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Whether from a Western or an Eastern view, if lack of shame becomes the public norm, our political system will break down, progressively and irreversibly.

sections.label: Committee finds Workers' Party cover-up
sections.summary: The Committee investigating Ms Raeesah Khan's transgressions unexpectedly found a cover-up by Workers' Party leaders, and Parliament must now act.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We thought the matter could be closed off straightforwardly, but there turned out to be a much larger problem.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And just like in the original Watergate affair, while investigating Ms Raeesah Khan’s transgressions, the Committee unexpectedly stumbled upon a cover-up by Workers' Party leaders, even more serious than the original offence.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But, now, with the findings before us, it is our responsibility, Parliament's responsibility, for the Members of Parliament (MPs) to take the necessary and appropriate course of action.

sections.label: Objection to First Motion limb
sections.summary: The objection to the First Motion concerns limb 2(c), which assumes the COP accepted a mitigatory point affecting Ms Raeesah Khan's fine.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As I explained in my speech, the reasons why we are objecting, particularly to the First Motion, is with regard to limb 2(c).

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And the understanding behind limb 2(c) is that there is something for which Ms Raeesah Khan's fine, the quantum of the fine is what it is because the assumption is the COP has accepted that there is a mitigatory point to be made.

sections.label: Draft wording versus Report wording
sections.summary: An initial draft said Mr Singh weaponised allegations about Ms Khan, while the Report at page 58 says he alleged mental health problems.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: The initial draft read as follows: "Mr Singh essentially weaponised unsubstantiated allegations that Ms Khan was unstable and unreliable and that she was prone to lying because of her mental health and this was connected to her being a sexual assault victim." But in the Report before this House, which is the only public report put out, at page 58, paragraph 176(4), it says: "Mr Singh then alleged that Ms Khan had mental health problems and suggested that she was predisposed to lying", so on and so forth.

sections.label: Weaponised word was speaker's characterisation
sections.summary: The speaker says 'weaponised' was his own characterisation, citing a Rice Media article, and that the Report did not use that word.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
sentences.text: I have a clarification to make after this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And I mentioned earlier that the word "weaponised" was my characterisation of what I made of that particular paragraph.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I cannot remember whether I read this specifically, but Rice Media has an article which says: "Now that the claims on Raeesah Khan's mental health have been refuted, how do you feel about weaponising an individual's mental health in an investigation?" So, generally, that was my characterisation of what I saw the COP Report was doing and, hence, the choice of my usage of the word "weaponised".

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I did not refer in my speech to saying that the Report specifically used the word "weaponised".

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I said, "the most egregious is the conclusion that in seeking a psychiatric evaluation for Ms Khan, I had somehow weaponised her condition".

sections.label: Loh Pei Ying's reservations messaged
sections.summary: Ms Loh Pei Ying had messaged him expressing grave reservations about the DP and Mr Singh's suppression of material facts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: First, that Ms Loh Pei Ying had messaged him to express grave reservations about the DP, as well as Mr Singh's suppression of material facts concerning his involvement to the DP.

sections.label: Loh Pei Ying WhatsApp message
sections.summary: On 2 November, the day the DP was formed, Ms Loh Pei Ying sent Mr Yudhisthra Nathan a WhatsApp message, also in evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: Another response I have is that, in fact, on the same day that the DP was formed, on 2 November, this is what Ms Loh Pei Ying said to Mr Yudhisthra Nathan via WhatsApp, also contemporaneous, also in evidence.

sections.label: Evidence placed before Public Prosecutor
sections.summary: All evidence and exhibits will be placed before the Public Prosecutor for consideration.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: So, these and other messages are in the Annexes, some of them are in the evidence and some of the messages were placed in front of Mr Singh and some of the other witnesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: So, in a sense, all the evidence, all the exhibits will be placed before the Public Prosecutor (PP).

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: And I welcome Mr Singh's support that all these will be placed before the PP to be considered so that he can clear his name and put his explanation out.

sections.label: Committee evidence referred to Prosecutor
sections.summary: All witness evidence was assessed by the Committee and placed in the Report, and materials will go to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: Be that as it may, all the evidence submitted by all witnesses was placed before the Committee, was referred to, we assessed the evidence, we came to our conclusions and we placed it into the Report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
sentences.text: But all materials, including materials that the relevant witnesses, including from the Workers' Party leadership, had submitted would be placed before the PP for consideration.

sections.label: Referral of new case to Prosecutor
sections.summary: The COP recommends referring the new case to the Public Prosecutor so parties can defend themselves.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Well, for me, suffice to say that to ignore the evidence is not an option.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Hence, the recommendation made by the COP to refer the new case to the Public Prosecutor is the right and best option.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In that way, the parties who were not the original subjects of the COP have a chance to defend themselves and clear their names.

sections.label: Referral of Faisal Manap and Pritam Singh
sections.summary: Ms Sylvia Lim will address the intended referral of Mr Faisal Manap and Mr Pritam Singh to the Public Prosecutor and argue for COP reforms.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Faisal Manap is not here.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I will touch on the referral, or intended referral, of Mr Faisal Manap and Mr Pritam Singh to the Public Prosecutor, and I will also argue why some reforms to the COP and its processes are much needed.

sections.label: COP finding on handwritten notes
sections.summary: At paragraph 237 of the Main Report, the COP finds the handwritten notes useful to its deliberations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: At paragraph 237 of the Main Report, the COP finds that my handwritten notes were useful to the Committee in its deliberations.

sections.label: COP misquoting evidence paragraph
sections.summary: The COP did not accurately quote paragraph 12554 when stating the speaker was clear a truth choice cannot be given to MPs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But if one looks at footnote 421, it refers to a particular paragraph of my evidence, which is as follows, paragraph 12554, where I said: "You see, it never crossed my mind and I cannot fathom this possibility that Pritam would have given her the option to choose between telling the truth or continuing the lie.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: That never crossed my mind and I do not believe it to be true." Sir, the COP did not quote this paragraph accurately when it stated that I was clear that a choice to tell the truth cannot be given to MPs.

sections.label: Omitted evidence paragraphs
sections.summary: The speaker says four vital paragraphs following the evidence the COP relied on were not included.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: When I referred back to the evidence that the COP relied on, I find that four vital paragraphs that immediately followed were not included, which are critical to properly understand my evidence.

sections.label: Referral to Public Prosecutor
sections.summary: The speaker notes a court conviction can disqualify an MP if the fine is $2,000 or more, unlike Parliament fines up to $50,000.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Next, Sir, I will touch briefly on the referral to the Public Prosecutor (PP) or the intended referral to the PP of Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Faisal Manap.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A Court conviction may prematurely terminate the service of an MP who has been duly elected by the people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is provided in Article 45 of the Constitution that convictions in a Court of law can disqualify an elected Member of Parliament from Parliament if the fine is $2,000 or more.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Contrast this with fines meted out by Parliament itself under the Parliament (Privileges, Immunities and Powers) Act, which can go up to $50,000 but will not disqualify an MP from continuing to serve this House.

sections.label: Committee opposition party members
sections.summary: The speaker says if the Committee's total strength remains eight Members, three should be from opposition parties.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If the Committee’s total strength is to remain at eight Members in all, then, three Members should be from opposition parties.

sections.label: Debate on Committee motion
sections.summary: The speaker says the debate intends to approve the Committee of Privileges' recommendation to fine Ms Raeesah Khan $35,000 and refer him and Mr Pritam Singh to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: (In Malay):   This debate intends to approve the Motion, in a nutshell, on the recommendation of the parliamentary Committee of Privileges for Ms Raeesah Khan to be fined $35,000, and also to refer me and my colleague Mr Pritam Singh to the Public Prosecutor for further investigation.

sections.label: Rejecting accusation and assuring residents
sections.summary: The speaker rejects the accusation that he and his colleagues advised Ms Raeesah Khan to continue to lie and assures Aljunied and Sengkang GRC residents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What I will say is that, first, I would like to once again reject the accusation that I, and both my colleagues, Mr Pritam Singh and Ms Sylvia Lim, advised Ms Raeesah Khan to continue to lie.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Next, I would like to assure residents of Aljunied GRC, especially residents of Kaki Bukit whom I have served for almost 11 years, that my services to you will not be affected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For Sengkang GRC residents, I would like to reiterate my statement on 2 December that I will work closely with the three Sengkang GRC Members of Parliament, Ms He Ting Ru, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Louis Chua in serving you, especially in matters related to Malay/Muslim community affairs.

sections.label: Faisal Manap evidence refusal
sections.summary: The speaker says Mr Faisal Manap's evidence was key and that he refused to answer a COP question eight times.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In this matter, the evidence of the hon Member Mr Muhamad Faisal bin Abdul Manap has been key to understanding the events that unfolded as stated in the COP Report.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: It is disappointing that Mr Faisal Manap has refused to answer a question put by the COP eight times.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: When Mr Faisal Manap gave evidence, he said that he met with Mr Pritam Singh and Ms Sylvia Lim on 7 and 8 December 2020; just two days before he was due to give evidence to the COP.

sections.label: Refusal to answer referred
sections.summary: The speaker understands the COP had no choice but to refer his refusal to answer to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Despite being told that such a refusal to answer may be an offence, he still did not want to answer.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Hence, I can understand why the COP had no choice but to refer his conduct to the Public Prosecutor for his refusal to answer.

sections.label: Independent Public Prosecutor investigation
sections.summary: The speaker says an independent body like the Public Prosecutor should investigate so both Members can present their fullest case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Let an independent body like the Public Prosecutor investigate, as this would allow both Members to present their fullest case and provide their own explanations.

sections.label: Singh and Faisal Manap testimony
sections.summary: The COP disbelieved parts of Mr Singh's testimony, raising possible perjury, while Mr Faisal Manap declined to answer questions, possibly contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As regards Mr Singh’s testimony, the COP has said that it has disbelieved several parts of it, thus giving rise to the possibility that the serious criminal offence of perjury had been committed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As regards Mr Faisal Manap’s testimony, he had declined to answer several questions that the COP had posed to him, which may amount to contempt of Parliament.

sections.label: Referring matters to PP
sections.summary: The speaker views referring the two matters to the PP, and possibly the Courts, as correct and a second or third chance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, my view is that it is the correct thing to do, as recommended by the COP, to refer these two matters to the PP and, if the PP deems necessary for these matters to go to the Court, then for them to go to the Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In fact, referring the matter to the PP affords Mr Singh and Mr Faisal Manap what may be seen as a second, even third bite of the cherry, because both the PP and the Courts, if it proceeds to the Courts, would consider all the facts anew.

sections.label: Protecting public interest and House
sections.summary: The speaker sees the Motions and any Court proceedings as protecting public interest and the House's integrity and standing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As is evident, the COP or the Government could not possibly have been aware of the facts underlying the Second Motion until they were disclosed in the COP proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I see these Motions and any Court proceedings that may follow as an exercise to protect the public interest and the integrity and the standing of this House, and as a reminder that Parliament and Parliamentarians must deal in the currency of truth and that a failure to do so must have consequences.

sections.label: Courts best forum
sections.summary: The speaker's view is that the Courts are the best forum to determine the facts and apply the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the circumstances, my view is that the best forum to determine the facts in these matters and to apply it to the law, is the Courts.

sections.label: COP recommends fines and referral
sections.summary: The COP recommended fining Ms Raeesah Khan and referring Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Faisal Manap to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: The COP has recommended fining Ms Raeesah Khan and referring WP Secretary-General Mr Pritam Singh and Vice-Chairman Faisal Manap to the Public Prosecutor for lying under oath and refusing to answer the COP's questions and showing contempt for Parliament, respectively.

sections.label: WP leaders guided Khan's narrative
sections.summary: The Workers' Party leaders guided Ms Khan to maintain her narrative and withheld their knowledge from the CEC.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party leaders also guided her to maintain her original narrative, resulting in her doubling down on the untruth in Parliament on 4 October, compounding her initial offence.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party then arranged for Ms Khan to assume full responsibility for both occasions where she lied, on 1 November, while obscuring the Workers' Party leaders' role in guiding her.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: The three Workers' Party leaders withheld from its CEC the fact that they had already known about Ms Khan's lies, and the guidance that had been given to her.

sections.label: COP findings on Singh and Manap
sections.summary: The COP found Mr Singh lied under oath and Mr Faisal Manap was in contempt of Parliament.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: On the whole the COP found Mr Singh to have lied under oath, while Mr Faisal Manap was in contempt of Parliament by refusing to answer the COP's questions.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: Who have been hurt by the Workers' Party leaders' machinations?

sections.label: Victims of sexual assault, patients
sections.summary: The passage names victims of sexual assault and mental health patients.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: Fourth, victims of sexual assault and mental health patients.

sections.label: Exploiting sympathy, numbing public
sections.summary: The passage states exploiting sympathy distracts the public and numbs them to lies and dishonesty.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: To exploit the public’s sympathy for the underdog and paint the COP as being politically-motivated not only distract the public from the core issue, but also seek to numb the public to lies and dishonesty gradually.

sentences.speaker: The Deputy Government Whip (Ms Sim Ann)
sentences.text: It is wrong to lie, and it is worse for a Member of Parliament to do so.

sections.label: COP Report on why Khan lied
sections.summary: Mr Singh said the COP did not want to find why Ms Khan lied, but the report has hundreds of pages on it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The second thing Mr Singh said was that the COP did not appear to want to get to the bottom of why Ms Khan lied in Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Actually, there are hundreds of pages in the COP Report that are all directed to why did she lie on 4 October.

sections.label: Factors Committee of Privileges considered
sections.summary: Mr Singh said uncorroborated testimony took centre stage, while the speaker listed factors the Committee of Privileges considered.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The next thing Mr Singh said was that what took centre stage was the uncorroborated testimony that she was instructed to lie.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I spent a great deal of time in my opening speech listing out what exactly the factors were that the Committee of Privileges took into account, in terms of corroborative testimony, contemporaneous evidence, written documents, the evidence of other witnesses, and whether or not something made sense.

sections.label: Documents included in COP Report
sections.summary: Tribunals need not include everything submitted, but the Report includes many documents from Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Tribunals, and in this case the COP, do not necessarily have to put in everything that was submitted, but they did include a lot of documents – the Report does include many documents submitted by Mr Singh, Ms Lim and Mr Faisal Manap.

sections.label: Composition of Committee of Privileges
sections.summary: Standing Order 100(7)(a)(i) states the Committee of Privileges consists of the Speaker as Chairman and seven nominated members.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The composition of the COP is dealt with in the Standing Orders of Parliament, in Standing Order 100(7), sub-paragraph (a)(i), "There shall be a Committee to be known as the Committee of Privileges to consist of the Speaker as Chairman and seven members to be nominated by the Committee of Selection as soon as may be after its appointment, in such manner as shall ensure that, so far as it is possible, the balance between the Government benches and the Opposition benches in Parliament is reflected in the Committee".

sections.label: Speeches missed core findings
sections.summary: The speeches did not address the core findings of the Committee of Privileges, which was why the truth took so long.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The speeches did not address the core findings of the Committee of Privileges, which was: why did it take so long to have the truth told to Parliament?

sections.label: No clear instruction to tell truth
sections.summary: The evidence is undisputed that no clear instruction was given to Raeesah to return to Parliament and tell the truth.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Because after all this evidence – and this is not disputed – there was no clear instruction from Mr Singh, or anybody else, to say, "Raeesah, please go back to Parliament and tell them the truth." Instead, there is this parsing of words, this "take ownership", "take responsibility", "I will not judge you".

sections.label: Unanswered pertinent questions remain
sections.summary: These pertinent questions have not been answered, leaving the situation for a decision on what to do.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I mean, these are questions that have not been answered, and these are pertinent questions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, that leaves us with a situation where we have to decide what to do.

sections.label: Referral to Public Prosecutor
sections.summary: Serious findings against Mr Singh and Mr Faisal Manap are referred to the Public Prosecutor, while other findings are held back.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And if you go back, you are going to have the same thing and, not only that, there are probably going to be aspersions cast on the new Committee of Privileges.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, for the more egregious, serious transgressions – in this case, the findings that Mr Singh had lied and that Mr Faisal Manap had prevaricated, refused to give documents, refused to answer questions – the recommendation is that those be referred to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And the other things, for example, that Ms Lim lied, that Mr Faisal Manap lied, those we hold back until the PP has decided what to do.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Report has highlighted things that we cannot ignore and we have to make a decision.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And referring Mr Singh and Mr Faisal Manap to the PP is the fairest thing to do because, if they maintain their innocence, they will have a chance to vindicate themselves.

sections.label: Clarifying vote on First Motion
sections.summary: Mr Singh is asked whether they would vote for the first two parts of the First Motion but not the $10,000 fine.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: What I am asking Mr Singh is whether he can clarify that they would be prepared to vote in favour of the first two parts of the First Motion, but not in favour of the last part, which imposes the $10,000 fine.

sections.label: WP voting on Motions
sections.summary: The WP will vote for Motion one 2(a) and 2(b), but no to 2(c) and Motion two, rejecting the COP findings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: Indeed, for Motion number one, with regard to 2(a) and 2(b), we will be voting in favour.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And then for 2(c), indeed, as Leader said that implicit in that, we are going to vote no, and she is right.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: For the very same reason, Leader of the House is right, Mr Faisal Manap and myself have no objections to being referred to the Public Prosecutor.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But – and this is a big "but" – we will still vote no to Motion number two, because in the same way it is implicit in Motion number one, 2(c), it is also implicit in the second paragraph of Motion number two that the basis of the referral to the PP arises from evidence uncovered at the COP; and we reject those findings.

sections.label: Lifting Standing Orders for votes
sections.summary: The Speaker is asked to lift Standing Orders so 2(a) and 2(b) pass unanimously and 2(c) is voted separately.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But there is a way to allow us to vote for 2(a) and 2(b), and remove 2(c) which is voted on separately, if we lift the Standing Orders.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And what I will do, with the Speaker's permission, is to ask to lift the Standing Orders in respect of the First Motion, to allow the votes for 2(a) and 2(b) to be taken, and then for 2(c) to be taken separately, which will then record that the first two were unanimously passed, and the third one was rejected by the WP.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I would not be seeking to lift the Standing Orders in respect of the Second Motion since Mr Singh has said that they would not be agreeing to any part of it, with the important caveat that they have put on record that he and Mr Faisal Manap are prepared to be referred to the Public Prosecutor to clear their names.
